cells.tense: The weighing and the saying sit close together right now — the answer comes out near when it settles.
cells.ask: Say the next answer out loud as soon as it settles, within the hour, even to a room that didn't ask.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day this looks like one direction named and left named the next morning. Someone asks what you're doing and you tell them, plainly, without running ten versions first. Thinking something through and thinking it to death are different, and you can feel where the line is.

What this steadiness can feed next is structure — a day that holds together because the decisions in it hold. Saying the next answer as soon as it settles shows you whether the direction carries weight once you stop editing it after the fact. What you get is the record of your own timing, kept where you can find it.

cells.tense: You're living a step ahead of what's actually been decided, running the exchange to its end before it starts.
cells.ask: Write the next single decision on one line, keep to that line for a full day, and make one move on the list you'd otherwise reorder again.
cells.core:
The pause turns into a room where everything gets weighed for the branch it might take. Nothing has been chosen because nothing has been left alone, and waiting for the right moment has started to cost the thing it was protecting.

On a good day it looks different: a direction named once and still named that way the next morning, with nobody checking whether it survived the night. Following a hope past the point where it's comfortable is what a day of already-chosen looks like here — trusting what you've set in motion to keep going without your permission. That's where the hour you've been paying out comes back.

cells.tense: You're parked at a threshold that closed behind you, holding words from a moment that's already gone.
cells.ask: Speak one true sentence to whoever asked, within a day, in whatever shape it comes out — even unfinished.
cells.core:
By the time someone needs the answer, the moment has passed, and the shortest true thing spoken out loud feels like stepping into open air. The weighing starts before any sentence gets built, so what's starved is the road from holding it to handing it over.

On an ordinary day this runs the other way: an answer surfaces and gets said while it's small, before the weighing can eat it. Satisfaction that comes from imagining something all the way through, and feeling it landed, is a different muscle than being asked to speak on command — and it's the one that reopens the road. That is what the direction has been waiting on.

cells.tense: You're steering while calling it reacting, and the direction is being settled right now, under your hands.
cells.ask: Name one decision set in motion by your own hand this week, out loud once, plainly, without calling it anything else.
cells.core:
The direction that's running is already real, just filed under a smaller name — what the job asked for, what had to be answered, the obvious next thing. Giving the deciding away is what has kept it unnamed.

On an ordinary day this looks like owning the call as you make it, without a story about who really decided. Naming one decision made by your own hand is the smallest exchange on the same line, and a plain exchange hands back what you've been paying to hand off. Fairness done naturally is a small, clear ledger: given and received, no tally kept.

attempts.check: The draft asserts that a chosen direction is actually being lived and kept whole; the record only says inner knowing is holding before it declares, which cannot by itself prove anything was chosen or preserved. A reader could reasonably say the knowing has not yet reached speech at all, rather than a direction being edited or abandoned. The asks survive that being wrong because each one only asks for one visible act of speaking or aligning a commitment, which still gives the person something usable even if the reading misses. The sentence that most serves the writer is the 'costs nothing' close in cell 4, since it is working to sell the not-straining line rather than showing the person the fix — I cut it in favor of a smaller plain line.

A reader could reasonably say the holding never resolves, and my healthy-picture sentences assume it does.
